slides.title: How The System Makes The Tables
slides.statement: You can explain how codes and kits decide the tables, and how each table is built, set and recorded.
slides.notes: Lesson outcome.

slides.title: How The System Makes The Tables
slides.line: Nia keeps the spreadsheet for her family's walking group, so when she heard Stage 4 was about tables, she thought it would be easy.
slides.notes: Nia keeps the spreadsheet for her family's walking group, so when she heard Stage 4 was about tables, she thought it would be easy. She planned to add columns as she went, and rename them whenever better names came to mind. Then she learned two facts about the build platform. Renaming a table or column destroys every row in it, and still reports success. And changing who can read a table after it is made costs a paid building turn. So she changed her approach. Plan every table first, set it right at birth, and write down why it exists.

slides.title: How The System Makes The Tables
slides.statement: A Schema Is The Plan Of Tables
slides.notes: Stage 4 is called Schema. A schema is the plan of the tables that hold the data: which tables exist, which columns each one has, and who may read or write them. A column is one field in a table, like a dog's name or a booking date. Stage 4 sits in the Rig room, together with Stage 5, and it is free. Nothing here is built by the paid builder. The tables are built by hand, then proved by reading them back, which is called a re-read. Free work now saves paid work later.

slides.title: How The System Makes The Tables
slides.statement: Codes And Kits Decide The Tables
slides.line: Where does the list of tables come from?
slides.notes: Where does the list of tables come from? Not from guessing. The kits chosen earlier each bring their own tables. K00, the floor, brings seven: tenants, tenant users, roles, permissions, consents, usage channels and events. K02, booking, adds bookings, availability slots and resources. The codes on the idea card then shape the columns. If TEN (0-6) is 2 or more, several businesses share the app, so every table holding a business's data needs a tenant id column, which says which business owns each row. A tenant is one business using the app.

slides.title: How The System Makes The Tables
slides.statement: A Spec First, Then Built By Hand
slides.line: Before anything is created, the tables and columns are written out as a spec, short for specification, saved as a CSV file.
slides.notes: Before anything is created, the tables and columns are written out as a spec, short for specification, saved as a CSV file. A CSV is a plain file of rows and columns that any program can open. The spec is never left as loose prose, because nobody can test a paragraph. Every name is checked against the naming standard, so one idea always has one name. Then the tables are built by hand, for free, and each one is read back to prove it exists exactly as written. A copied base is also swept for ghost columns, ones it inherited but does not use.

slides.title: How The System Makes The Tables
slides.statement: Access Modes Say Who Can Read
slides.line: Every table has an access mode, a setting that says who may read and write its rows.
slides.notes: Every table has an access mode, a setting that says who may read and write its rows. Here are some examples. Public means anyone can read, even when signed out. User scoped means each row belongs to the signed-in person who made it. Anonymous writable means a stranger can add rows without signing in. A role gate limits a table to people with a given role, such as staff. The access mode is set when the table is created, which is free. Changing it afterwards is a billed builder turn. So the mode is decided on paper first.

slides.title: How The System Makes The Tables
slides.statement: Probe Every Table While Signed Out
slides.line: Deciding a mode is not the same as having it.
slides.notes: Deciding a mode is not the same as having it. So each table gets an anonymous probe. A probe is a test request, and anonymous means it is sent with nobody signed in, the way a stranger on the internet would arrive. If a table is meant to be private and the probe gets rows back, something is wrong, and it is fixed before going further. The codes set what is allowed. Litterline has POST (0-2) at 0, so no table should take writes from a stranger. VIEW (0-2) at 1 means only link-holders may read anything signed out.

slides.title: How The System Makes The Tables
slides.statement: Every Table Gets A Register Row
slides.line: The last piece is the table register, section 4.0 of the app's document.
slides.notes: The last piece is the table register, section 4.0 of the app's document. Every table gets one row in it, with the reason the table exists, its role gate and who may write to it. This sounds like paperwork, but it prevents a costly mistake. A table is never removed just because no code seems to read it. Removing a table needs a person's dated ruling. Without a register, a table that looks unused might hold the one record a business needs on inspection day, and deleting it would be very hard to undo.

slides.title: How The System Makes The Tables
slides.statement: Never Rename, Add And Migrate Instead
slides.line: One rule from the duties file is worth learning by heart.
slides.notes: One rule from the duties file is worth learning by heart. Never rename a table or column. A rename destroys every row and still returns a success message, so nobody notices until the data is gone. If a name must change, the safe way is to add the new column, copy the data across, which is called migrating, and leave the old one unread. Plan, spec, build by hand, set the mode, probe, record. That is how Stage 4 makes its tables. Now a short recap before we meet the walls.

slides.notes: Answer: B. A schema is the plan of the tables, their columns and who may read or write them.

slides.title: Walls And Table Tests
slides.statement: You can name the eight walls and describe the table tests that must pass before the Schema gate.
slides.notes: Lesson outcome.

slides.title: Walls And Table Tests
slides.line: Theo's cousin works at a grooming salon.
slides.notes: Theo's cousin works at a grooming salon. One morning, the booking app the salon used showed her another salon's client list, names and phone numbers included. It was fixed within a day, but the trust was gone. When Theo started helping to plan Trimtable, he wanted to be sure it could never do that. At first he wrote, the data is private, in his notes. Then he realised that sentence proved nothing. What he needed was a test for each table that could actually fail, run from outside, with a date beside the result.

slides.title: Walls And Table Tests
slides.statement: A Wall Keeps Two Parties Apart
slides.line: In the factory, a wall is a rule that keeps two parties' data apart.
slides.notes: In the factory, a wall is a rule that keeps two parties' data apart. The simplest picture has three walls. Owner from owner keeps one reseller's businesses away from another reseller's. Business from business keeps one salon's records away from the next salon's. Customer from customer keeps one customer's details private inside a single business. The third wall always sits inside the second, never instead of it: check the business first, then the customer. Trimtable has no reseller above it, so the first wall has nobody on the other side yet.

slides.title: Walls And Table Tests
slides.line: The full set has eight walls, numbered W1-W8, and most codes on the idea card point to one.
slides.notes: The full set has eight walls, numbered W1-W8, and most codes on the idea card point to one. W1 is the brand wall, between businesses. W2 is the member wall, between customers. W3 is the layer-above wall, for parties sitting above a business. W4 is the staff wall, for roles, guests and view-as access. W5 is the membership wall, about who can join and belong, and whose name is shown. W6 is the public wall, for strangers who are signed out. W7 is the data-out wall, for data leaving the app. W8 is the sensitivity hold, for health or children's data.

slides.title: Walls And Table Tests
slides.statement: Each Table Gets The Right Test
slides.line: Stage 4 ends with table tests, section 4.4 of the document.
slides.notes: Stage 4 ends with table tests, section 4.4 of the document. The test depends on the kind of table. Application tables hold a business's own records, like bookings. Each one gets a brand-wall read: sign in as tenant A and try to read tenant B's rows. Tenant A must see none. User tables hold one person's own things. Each one gets a user-wall read: one user must not see another user's rows. Control tables hold the app's own settings, and each gets an anonymous read, sent signed out, which has to return 401.

slides.title: Walls And Table Tests
slides.line: 401 is a status code, a number a web server sends back with every answer.
slides.notes: 401 is a status code, a number a web server sends back with every answer. 401 means the request was refused because nobody is signed in. For a control table, that is exactly the answer you want a stranger to get. If the anonymous read returns 200 instead, which means success, and hands back rows, the table is open to the whole internet. That is a stop. The fix comes before anything else, and then the test is run again until it returns 401. A pass is only a pass when the stranger gets nothing.

slides.title: Walls And Table Tests
slides.line: Some tables are shared on purpose.
slides.notes: Some tables are shared on purpose. Imagine one dog's record that two breeders both hold a claim on, with each allowed to see different fields. A field is one column in one row. A shared row carries no tenant id, so a normal row-level test looks for a tenant tag, finds none, and reports all clear, while the wrong fields leak. That is why the rule says a row-level test passes while leaking. On a shared table the leak test must be field-level: check that each claim sees only the fields it is allowed to see.

slides.title: Walls And Table Tests
slides.statement: Every Test Has A Dated Result
slides.line: A test without a result is just a hope.
slides.notes: A test without a result is just a hope. So the stage is finished only when every Launch table and every Base table has at least one test with a dated result. Launch tables are the ones the first version uses. Base tables are the ones that come with the base the app started from. The tests are run from outside, as a real visitor would, not by asking the builder whether it worked. A sentence in the notes, such as the data is private, never counts. Only a test that could fail, and did not, counts.

slides.title: Walls And Table Tests
slides.statement: The Schema Gate Passes By Itself
slides.notes: Then comes the Schema gate. It sits between Stage 4 and Stage 5 and asks: tables probed, names re-read? Like the Base gate, it is automatic. When every Stage 4 checklist line is done, and no section of the document still says pending, the engine moves the app on without anyone clicking yes. That only works because the tests are plain. A probe returned 401 or it did not. A name matches the spec or it does not. Next comes Stage 5, where test businesses and test people are set up. First, the recap.

slides.title: Quick Check
slides.q: Which wall keeps one business's data away from another business?
slides.notes: Answer: A. W1, the brand wall, sits between businesses.
